title: Emberfall dialogue
descriptions:
The shadows here are deep, and hope is a rare guest in these halls. Yet I see a glimmer of light in your eyes, stranger.

I am bound to this darkness, but perhaps you are not. If your heart still knows pity, I beg a small boon of you.

Bring me %s.

%s

Grant me this, and I shall share what little aid I can still offer.

Keep to this side of the pump. The guards cannot see us from the upper walk. I used to service these valves before the regent turned the crews into prisoners.

I need %s.

%s

Bring it here and I can help with your equipment. They took my workshop, but they have not taken what I know.

You there - halt. You have the look of a free soul about you, and that is a rare and dangerous thing in these deeps.

I have nothing to offer but words, and those are cheap in Angband. But I have a need, and you may have the means.

Bring me %s.

%s

Do this, and I will repay the kindness as best I can. I have not forgotten all my skill.

Your boots are not marked for a work gang. Good. That means you can reach stores they will never let me near. I have been saving my strength for an opening, but I am missing something.

Can you bring me %s?

%s

I have a trade to offer in return, if we can keep the overseer out of it.

Do not be afraid. I was a man once, before the chains and the dark. I still am, though they would have me forget it.

The overseers leave me alive because my hands are useful, but my spirit is my own, and it cries out for one mercy.

Bring me %s.

%s

In return I shall put these calloused hands to work for you.

Please wait. I am not reaching for a weapon; I need you to hear me before the next shift begins. I worked the ferry yards before this place, and I know how to make a useful repair.

First I need %s.

%s

If you can find it, I will put that knowledge to work for you.

Another wanderer in the pits. I would warn you to turn back, but no road leads out of Angband save through it.

I have laboured here longer than I care to reckon. My strength fades, but my wits have not yet been broken.

If you could find me %s, it would be a lifeline in this drowning dark.

%s

Help me, and I will help you. That is an honest bargain, even here.

I have counted six changes of guard since they last opened the service hatch. There may be a way through it, but I cannot make the attempt as I am.

Would you find me %s?

%s

Help me prepare, and I will do what I can for the gear carrying you through this place.

Quiet - the guards have just passed. Listen, I have not much time to speak.

They have worked me near to death, but I am still breathing, and where there is breath there is a chance. I need your help.

Bring me %s.

%s

I can still ply a trade, and I will use it in your favour.

The hammering covers our voices for a moment. Listen: I have hidden a little room behind the scrap bins, enough to work without the guards looking over my shoulder.

What I need is %s.

%s

Bring it while the shift is changing. I can repay you with work they do not own.

I see from your bearing that you are no thrall. That alone gives me courage to ask what I am about to ask.

They took everything from me - my home, my name, my kin. All I have left is the hope that someone, someday, might show me a scrap of kindness.

Bring me %s.

%s

Do this, and what skill these worn hands still possess is yours.

I still remember the inventory marks from my old quay. Sometimes I trace them on the wall to keep my hands from forgetting their work. You look as though you might get back to those cities.

Before you go, could you bring me %s?

%s

I cannot travel with you, but I can make my skill useful to your journey.

Ai! A star in the darkness! Do my eyes deceive me, or do I look upon one of the Free Peoples walking these accursed paths?

I am weary, kinsman, weary beyond the counting of years. The Shadow lies heavy upon my fea.

Yet, if you would show mercy to one who has lost all, bring me %s.

%s

In return, I shall speak to you of ancient works and secrets long forgotten by the world above.

The return lamps have been dark so long that I nearly mistook you for a memory. Come closer, away from the listening pipe. I kept the instrument records before they brought me below.

I need %s.

%s

If you can help, I will share the workshop knowledge I have kept hidden from the overseers.

Stay your step, wanderer. Not all who dwell here are foes, though the iron and shadow would have it so.

Once I walked beneath stars and knew the names of every tree from root to crown. Now I count the hours by the dripping of water and the turning of the wheel.

If compassion yet moves your heart, bring me %s.

%s

It would ease my captivity, and I would repay you with such knowledge as I still possess.

There is a safe board beside the drain; stand there. I know which parts of this gallery are still sound because I helped inspect them before the occupation.

Can you obtain %s for me?

%s

I can offer what I remember of the old equipment and the ways it was made.

A… free walker? Here, in the deep places? I thought my eyes had at last surrendered to the dark, but no - you are real.

I was taken from the green lands long ago, and the song has all but left my voice. Still, I remember enough to be of use.

If it is within your power, bring me %s.

%s

I shall repay such grace with whatever craft the long years have not stripped from me.

You found this chamber without a guard escort. Then the lower passages are not completely closed. I have been waiting for someone who could carry a request beyond this wall.

Please bring %s.

%s

There is still useful work in these hands, and I will use it for you.

Daro! Do not strike. I am no servant of the Enemy, though my chains would give the lie to that claim.

There was a time when my people sang the world into shape. Now I sing only to keep madness at bay. But I have not yet fallen.

I ask only this: bring me %s.

%s

Grant me this, and the old knowledge shall be yours - such of it as endures in a captive heart.

Do not follow the cable on the floor; it leads to the alarm. I pulled it loose so we could speak here. The guards make me maintain their instruments, but I have kept some procedures out of their books.

I would trade that knowledge for %s.

%s

Will you help me?

Hush - speak softly. The walls have ears, and the servants of the Enemy are cunning beyond measure.

I have dwelt in these pits since before the sun last touched my face. My strength wanes, but my memory is long, and I remember things of power and beauty.

If pity stirs in your breast, bring me %s.

%s

In exchange I will impart to you a portion of the Elder craft - small, perhaps, but not without worth.

The old survey marks are still under the soot. I read them when I need to remember that these were once service works, built by people rather than masters.

Would you bring me %s?

%s

In return, I can explain some of the craft that survived with those marks.

You move as one who still knows the taste of open air. How I envy you.

I was a maker once - a shaper of fair things in the halls of my people. Now my forge is cold and my tools are rust. But the skill lives on in these fingers, if barely.

Would you bring me %s?

%s

I would give you something in return - a gift of craft that the darkness has not yet devoured.

I used to fit the signal crystals in the western docks. Even now I find myself checking the alignment of every lamp they make me clean. There may still be something I can teach you.

First, I need %s.

%s

Bring it here, and the next piece of useful knowledge will leave this prison with you.

You return... and I see you bear the burden I spoke of. Can it be true? Have you brought %s to this wretched place?

%s

If you would part with it, my gratitude would be boundless.

You made it back. Is that %s you found? I kept the work space ready in case you returned.

%s

Will you give it to me? I will do the work we agreed on.

I see it upon you - %s! My heart leaps at the sight.

%s

Will you surrender it to one whose freedom hangs by a thread?

That is %s, just what I asked for. Keep your voice down; the next guard is near the stairs.

%s

Can you spare it for me?

Wait - is that %s I spy? I have dreamed of such a thing through many dark watches.

%s

Say the word, and it shall not be given in vain.

I recognize %s among your gear. I was beginning to think the stores had all been emptied.

%s

If you can hand it over, I am ready to repay the help.

By all that is still good in this world - you carry %s! I can scarcely believe my fortune.

%s

Would you part with it? I swear upon my people that the debt will be repaid.

You brought %s through all those checkpoints. I have not forgotten the bargain.

%s

Will you leave it with me?

Hold - I recognise what you carry. That is %s, unless my eyes have wholly failed me.

%s

If you would spare it, I will see that the kindness is returned.

Wait before you move on. You are carrying %s, and it would make a real difference here.

%s

Can you give it to me? My tools are ready for your equipment.

You have it - %s! I can see it plain as day, and my heart almost bursts with hope.

%s

Will you give it to me? I will put my hands and my wits at your service in thanks.

There it is: %s. I checked the hiding place again, and it is still safe enough to work.

%s

Will you let me have it? I can return the favor now.

You have returned, and the light of the stars seems to follow you. And... yes, I sense you carry %s.

%s

Is it for me? Will you grant this kindness to a fading spirit?

You returned to the right chamber. I can see %s in your gear.

%s

Will you give it to me? I have prepared the knowledge I promised you.

Ai, you have come again, and you bring with you %s! Even here, hope endures.

%s

Will you part with it for my sake?

That is %s. I recognize the shape even under this poor light.

%s

Can you spare it? We can finish our exchange before the inspection.

My heart quickens - can it be? You bear %s! The very air around you seems brighter for it.

%s

If you would bestow it upon me, I shall not soon forget the gift.

You found %s after all. I have kept the useful records in my head while waiting.

%s

Will you hand it over so I can begin?

Na vedui! At last, a kindness beyond hope. You carry %s, and its presence alone is a balm.

%s

Will you yield it to one whose need is great?

I was listening for the overseer, but it is you at the door, carrying %s.

%s

Can you leave it here? I am ready to do my part.

The light follows you still, and upon you I perceive %s. A thread of hope in a tapestry of ruin.

%s

If you can spare this boon, my craft - such as it is - shall be devoted to your cause.

The guards have not searched this corner today. We have time to exchange %s for the help I offered.

%s

Will you give it to me?

Ai, can it be? %s! My fea trembles at the sight. Even in Angband, the world is not wholly bereft of grace.

%s

Will you give it to one who has all but forgotten the sun?

Yes, %s is what I needed. Please keep it covered until you are beside me.

%s

If you can part with it, I can pass on the old craft now.

You... you have brought it? I had not dared to hope.

My thanks, stranger. You have done a kinder deed than you know. May your courage not fail you in the trials to come.

In payment, such as I can make, I will give you what craft or lore I have not forgotten.
You kept your word. I can make use of this before the next shift. Let me repay you with the trade I learned in the ferry yards; that part of my life still belongs to me.

It is done. You are a finer soul than any master I have served in these halls.

I had thought all kindness perished when I was thrown into this pit, but you have proven me wrong.

Take what I can give - some cunning of hand and eye that the long years of labour have taught me.
That will help. For once, something useful came into this chamber without an order from a guard. Bring your gear closer and I will do my part of the bargain.

I will not weep - tears are a luxury I cannot afford - but know that you have given me something more precious than gold.

For a moment I remember what it was to be free, and that is enough.

Here - let me set my hands to your gear. It is the least I can do.
I had nearly stopped planning for tomorrow. This gives me a reason to start again. Let me work on your equipment while my hands are steady.

You risked much to bring this to a wretch like me, and I will not forget it.

When I was a craftsman in the daylight world, my work was honest and strong. The dark has not stolen that from me entirely.

Let me put what remains of my old skill to your benefit.
You took a risk for someone the regent would never count. I will remember it. Here is what an old workshop hand can offer in return.

There are no words - not in the common tongue, nor in any speech I know - that can repay what you have done.

But words are not all I have. These hands still know their trade, battered though they are.

Come, let me work upon whatever you carry. It is the only coin I can offer, and I give it gladly.
Thank you. I can hide this where the inspection will miss it. Now let me show you a piece of work the overseers have never managed to take from me.

A good deed in a foul place. My old mother used to say that kindness is the only wealth that grows when you give it away.

She was right, and you have proven it.

Now let me see what I can do for you - I may be a slave, but my craft is still my own.
A fair exchange in a place built on taking. I needed that more than you know. Hold your equipment still; I can repay the help with useful work.

Elen síla lúmenn' omentielvo! You have my deepest thanks.

Long have I lacked such kindness in this forsaken place. May the stars shine upon your road, and may your hand be swift and your heart steadfast.

In return I will share with you what lore and craft remain to me, dim though my memory has become in these pits.
This will last me through another shift. Thank you for returning. I have kept the instrument procedures clear in my memory, and I will share what can help you now.

Hannon le, mellon. The grace of the Valar is not yet wholly spent if such mercy can be found in Morgoth's domain.

My spirit is lifted, if only for a moment, and in that moment I am myself again.

Let me share with you a fragment of the ancient craft - a gift from one who may soon pass beyond all circles of the world.
The guards would call this missing inventory. I call it help freely given. Let me return it with the craft I learned before these galleries became a prison.

Le hannon, le hannon. Words fail where gratitude is too deep for speech.

You have rekindled an ember I thought quenched forever. Even if this body fails, the memory of your kindness will not fade from the song.

Accept what I can offer - a whisper of the old craft, shaped in better days.
You brought more than a useful object: you proved a promise can still be kept here. Take this knowledge with you; I would rather see it used than hidden.

You walk in the shadow of Morgoth himself, yet you carry light with you. That is no small thing.

I have seen ages pass in this darkness, and few deeds have touched me so. May the stars remember your name when all other names are forgotten.

Come - let me share what lore I have. It is poor coin for such a gift, but it is all I possess.
Thank you. I had begun to measure every visitor by the trouble they brought. You have given me a different measure. Here is the workshop knowledge I promised.

Gi nathlam hí. You honour me beyond all deserving.

In the long dark I have felt my fea diminish, a candle guttering in a gale. Yet your gift has steadied the flame, if only for a breath.

Let me repay you with a remnant of Noldorin craft - ancient and worn, yet still sharp.
My hands have remembered the work all this time. Now someone besides the regent will benefit from it. Let me repay you before the overseer returns.

A… tear? I had forgotten the Eldar could still weep. Forgive me - it has been long since anyone showed me such generosity.

The world beyond these walls grows dim in my memory, but the old skills remain. They are etched into my hands deeper than any chain.

Take what I offer. It is given freely, from a heart that you have made whole again, if only for a moment.
I can picture my old bench again, down to the worn edge beside the lamp. The skill is still there. Take what I can teach you and put it to use outside this cell.
With it I could scrape away the slag and filth about my chain-bolt, and perhaps find some hidden weakness in the stone.
A shovel would clear the packed slag from my chain-bolt. I want to see whether the stone beneath it has cracked.
With it I might loosen the stones about my fetter, and dig a little hollow wherein to hide myself when the guards are hunting.
I could dig around the fetter and make a covered space behind the loose blocks, somewhere the guards might overlook.
With it I may read the ways of these tunnels and avoid the pits and runes that the Orcs forget, for the dark here is a snare.
A lantern would let me read the survey marks and avoid the abandoned pits and warning signs in these tunnels.
With it I could steal through the blackness when the fires are quenched, and not stumble into chasms or the lash of the watch.
I need a light for the hours when the furnaces go cold. Without one, an unnoticed gap or patrol can end any attempt to move.
With it the smarting of wounds may be eased, that my hands do not tremble and my thoughts do not wander into madness.
The wounds keep my hands shaking. A healing herb would ease them enough for me to work and think clearly.
With it I could bind up the sores of the whip and the iron, and drive away the fever that has been set upon me.
I could treat the sores left by the collar and whip, and bring down the fever before the next shift.
With it I would set a clean light against the Shadow; the wood of mallorn remembers the West, and darkness draws back from such flame.
Its clean flame would give me a reliable light apart from the guard lamps. That wood burns well even in this bad air.
With it I would keep a true flame beside me, for the strange glamour of this place hates a light that is not of their making.
I could keep a steady flame beside the work space. The uncertain lights here make every small task harder.
With it a hurt that has gone black with poison may yet be cleansed, and my strength saved from a slow fading.
The wound has darkened with poison. A healing potion might clear it before it takes the strength I have left.
With it a wound that will not close may be stayed, and I might live to see another hour unchained of pain.
A healing potion could help close this stubborn wound and give me a little time without the pain.
With it I would not strike at the innocent, but keep a last defence, and a blade to cut cord or chain when a slender hope arises.
I need a small blade for cord and bindings, and something to defend myself with if the chance to leave comes.
With it I could sever rope or leather, and if the worst befall, keep one sharp edge between myself and the tormentors.
I could cut rope or leather with it, and keep an edge between myself and a guard if there is no other way.
With it I might move as once I moved beneath leaves and stars, unseen of captains and their hounds, and so slip from bondage for a time.
A cloak could hide my outline from the watch and its hounds while I move between the work chambers.
With it I could hide from the eye and the cold, for these deep ways gnaw at bone and the overseers see all who stand bare.
I need cover from the cold as well as the patrols. The open galleries leave me exposed to both.
With them I may tread in silence again, and not wake the watchers when I must pass between shadowed doors.
Boots would help me cross the service landings quietly, without alerting the watchers at the doors.
With them my feet would not bleed upon the stone, and if a door is left unbarred I could run before the cry is raised.
My feet are bleeding on the rough floor. With boots I might reach an open door before anyone could stop me.
With it I can endure the long watches when no crust is thrown to us, for even the Eldar are not beyond hunger in these pits.
A sustenance herb would carry me through the shifts when they withhold our rations.
With it I could master hunger for a while, and not be driven to folly when they starve us to obedience.
I could quiet my hunger long enough to think, instead of letting starvation make the next decision for me.
With it the strength that has been drained by torment may be rekindled, and I may remember myself for a little while.
I need to recover the strength this work has drained, enough to trust my own hands again.
With it I might recover what the Dark has stolen from my limbs, and stand straighter beneath their burden.
A restoration herb might give my weakened limbs back the strength to carry their load.
With it the veils upon my mind may be lifted, and the dreams they weave may be scattered like mist before the morning.
Clarity would help me separate what is happening from the visions and confused thoughts this place brings.
With it I could cast out the madness of fear and whispering shadows, and think clearly when the hour of choice comes.
I need a clear head when the next opening comes. These frightened, wandering thoughts could cost me that chance.
With it I could keep a small flame clean and steady, and remember for a while that light was made for more than the watchfires of Angband.
Oil would keep the lamp burning steadily through a whole watch instead of failing in the middle of work.
With it I could nurse a lamp through the dead watches, when a stumble in the black means the lash or the pit.
I could keep a lamp alive through the dark hours and see the floor before a misstep brings the guards.
With it I could carry one honest flame into the black ways, and not go wholly blind beneath the earth.
A torch would give me portable light for passages the fixed lamps no longer reach.
With it I could find a gate, a crack, any path not barred by iron, before the dark swallows my nerve.
I could search for a loose gate or crack in the walls without feeling for every step in darkness.
With it I could quiet the hunger that hollows my strength, and keep enough life in my limbs to endure the next labour.
Bread would quiet the hunger and leave me enough strength for the work they will demand next.
With it I could put strength back into my body; the scraps our masters cast us scarcely keep a man standing.
The rations barely keep me standing. Dried meat would put some strength back into my body.
I ask only to taste it once more, and remember the clean air beneath the trees before iron and darkness became all my world.
Those wafers were made for long journeys. A little food that lasts could help me endure here, and remind me what travel felt like.
With it I might yet endure a little longer, and do some small good before all light is quenched.
It would help me survive a little longer and keep enough strength to offer something useful in return.

You awaken in darkness. No name. No memory. Only a quiet ache of courage deep inside you, like embers buried beneath ash.
A pump starts somewhere beyond the wall. You wake with your hand closed around an absent railing. Your name is missing, but the instinct to get someone safely through a door remains.
Far below, Morgoth waits upon his throne—iron-dark and crowned in flame. Upon his brow shine three Silmarils, stolen stars. He senses your stirring. He knows you will come.
Below the tide cities, Varkesh has locked three dawnseeds into a command crown. The weather engine feeds his fortress while the reservoirs above lose their forecasts and their water.
Far above, beyond the shadows of Angband, the Valar watch silently. They offer no guidance, yet their presence fills you with strength—and dread.
The Nine Custodians receive your return signal. They are surviving operators and technical records of the failed engine, working with equipment that no longer meets its own safety limits.
You will return many times, each death and rebirth etched into the endless stone halls of Mandos. Each fall will draw your spirit deeper into shadow, closer to a doom from which you cannot escape.
The recall loom can rebuild a body around what remains of your memoryprint. Each death forces another recovery, and each recovery risks losing a detail that once made your life your own.
Yet each victory—each Silmaril wrested from Morgoth's crown—will brighten the Valar's hope, even as your soul grows thinner, your strength fading with every triumph.
A recovered dawnseed can restart a dead part of the weather system. Bringing one out also puts a heavier load through your return line. Repair and survival do not always ask the same thing of you.
You envy the Edain, whose Gift from Ilúvatar frees them from the bonds of Mandos and the world. Yet you do not know if such release can ever be yours. You do not know who—or even what—you truly are.
Some records end when their bearers die; others remain trapped in the recall cycle. You do not yet know why yours was preserved, or what happened during the evacuation it cannot fully remember.

For each time you awaken, you will carry the names of heroes beloved and feared—bright spirits, fiery hearts, proud kings and exiles, wanderers beneath sun and stars, whose courage you borrow, but whose fates are not your own.

The custodians keep training records from the people who built, guarded, and repaired the tide cities. Each return lets you work through a different record, taking its skills and its difficult habits into the deep.
This is the trial set by the Valar: to walk the narrow way between shadow and light, to bear the borrowed glory of the great, and to win back at last the name that was taken from you.

The descent has a practical purpose: recover the dawnseeds and restore the engine. Somewhere along that work, the broken record may also yield the name of the person who stayed behind at the flood gates.
Now the path before you opens, and your trial begins.
The return chamber opens. Beyond it, the first service passage is waiting.
You wake again in the dark, nameless and unremembered — a spirit set by the Valar to their long trial: to live the War of the Jewels once more, in a shape that is not your own.
The recall chamber has restored your body before it has restored your name. The custodians offer a surviving training record to carry through your next descent.

In the Elder Days, when the Two Trees of Valinor were slain and their light failed, Morgoth the great Enemy stole the Silmarils — the three holy jewels wrought by Fëanor, in which that light yet lived — and fled north to Angband, his fortress of iron beneath the triple peaks of Thangorodrim. There he set the Jewels in an iron crown and sat enthroned in darkness, walled about by orcs, balrogs, and dragons.

For the Silmarils Fëanor swore his terrible Oath, and the Noldor forsook the Blessed Realm and came in exile to Beleriand to make war upon the Enemy. They raised proud kingdoms and held Angband under siege through long years — yet their valour was ever shadowed by the Kinslaying at Alqualondë and the Doom of Mandos that followed them.

They did not fight alone. The Sindar, Grey-elves who dwelt beneath the stars of Beleriand long before the Noldor came, took up arms in the Elven realms and at the Havens of the Falas — though hidden Doriath, girdled by the power of Melian, held apart behind its enchanted bounds. The Naugrim, Dwarves of the Blue Mountains, forged matchless mail and axes and marched to the great battles. And the Edain, the first Men over the mountains, swore friendship to the Eldar and spent their brief, valiant lives in the war, winning undying renown.

The tide cities depended on a weather engine: reservoirs, pressure towers, and a network of signals that gave every quay time to prepare for a storm. Its operators became the Nine Custodians, keeping people and machinery working together across the changing water.

Varkesh seized the lower works during the Furnace Breach. He mounted three dawnseeds in a command crown and diverted their current to Karth Vault. The forecasts stopped. Relief gates failed to open, and the evacuations left whole districts under water.

The survivors came from many trades. Glasswright crews knew the engine instruments; Reedwalkers knew the changing marsh paths; Deep Masons kept foundations and tunnels sound; Tideborn communities supplied boats, provisions, and new workers. Their records still hold the skills needed for a repair. No single crew can finish it alone.

Choose now whose name you will wear — whose courage, whose grief, whose doom you carry down into Angband. Each Silmaril wrested from the iron crown brightens the Valar's hope, though your spirit thins; and in the borrowed glory of another you may, at last, remember your own forgotten name.

Choose the training record you will carry into Karth Vault. Its strengths and burdens will shape this attempt. Each dawnseed brought out repairs part of the engine, while each return may recover another piece of your missing life.

The Noldor are the High Elves of the West, deep in lore and craft, who dwelt in the light of Valinor. For love of the stolen Silmarils -- and, for some, bound by the dreadful Oath of Feanor -- they returned to Middle-earth in exile to make war upon Morgoth. Proud, mighty, and gifted, they raised shining kingdoms and forged wondrous things, yet a doom of sorrow and kinstrife shadows their valour. Their lineages descend from three lords: Feanor, Fingolfin, and Finarfin.

The Glasswrights built the instruments that measured storms and carried commands between reservoirs. They organized their work into Furnace, Breakwater, and Lantern Houses, each preserving a different balance of practical skills. The breach scattered their workshops and left dangerous unfinished contracts behind. Their records offer powerful training, along with the habits that once divided them.

The Sindar are the Grey-elves of Beleriand, kindred of the Eldar who never crossed the Sea but lingered under the stars of Middle-earth. Masters of song, woodcraft, and secret ways, they ruled the woven realm of Doriath and the havens of the Falas. Theirs is a quieter wisdom than the Noldor's, deep-rooted and enduring, though wars not of their making press hard upon their twilight land.

The Reedwalkers lived between the fixed gauges, where a channel could change before the next survey arrived. They used song signals, close observation, and hidden paths to keep the marsh settlements connected. After the engine failed, that local knowledge often mattered more than any official chart. Their records favor an attentive, adaptable approach.

The Naugrim, the Dwarves, are the hardy smith-folk who dwell in halls of stone beneath the mountains. Strong and stubborn, secretive yet steadfast, they are unmatched in the working of metal and gem. Their axes are feared and their mail is peerless; greed and grievance can stir them, but a Dwarf-friend has no truer ally in the long war against the Shadow.

The Deep Masons built the dry chambers beneath the tide cities and maintained the service ways that linked them. They judged a promise by whether its work survived the next flood. Their records preserve strength, craftsmanship, and the stubborn attention needed to repair a structure while others are still using it.

The Edain are the Men of the Three Houses, mortal and short-lived, who came over the mountains into Beleriand and allied themselves with the Eldar against Morgoth. Brief their years, but bright their valour; their deeds outrun their span and live on in song. Bound to the Elves by love and sorrow, they carry hope into the dark beyond the reach of the Eldar's fading.

The Tideborn rebuilt on the banks exposed after the cities broke. They supplied the ferries, food, and labor that kept isolated survivors connected. Their lives were shorter than the engine records they inherited, but each new crew learned quickly from the last. Their training favors endurance and action when there is no time for another council.
